On the 15-minute chart: price sweeps liquidity, shifts structure (MSS), returns to the nearest fair value gap and reacts, and only then does it enter, and only if the site's other methods read the same way. The stop sits beyond the sweep, the target is twice the stop.

The sequence: (1) price sweeps the last swing high or low and closes back, (2) it closes beyond the opposite swing (MSS), (3) it returns to the fair value gap that move left, or the order block if there is none, (4) a candle closes back out of it, (5) at least {0} more of the site's methods read that side than the other. The stop is usually $5–20 away: on a small account set your risk under "Trade size and stop" below; when the minimum lot does not fit, it does not enter. One or two trades a week on average: few, with a high bar.

Checked on three years of 15-minute candles (with $0.30 cost). On its own the pattern showed no edge (Profit Factor 0.85–1.08). Only when the reading agreed: 161 trades in the first 70%, 45% won, PF 1.37; 55 trades in the last 30%, 45%, PF 1.49. Entries against the reading lost (PF 0.51–0.95). Limits: a calculation on candle data, not real trading; it was picked from several variants, so real results are likely to be lower. Demo account first.

It enters when at least {0} methods back the side and outnumber the other (change the number in "Methods that must agree" below). The stop comes from the 1-hour ATR, so it is usually $10–25 away: at 0.01 lots a losing trade costs about that many dollars. That is a lot for a small account, so set your risk in $ or % under "Trade size and stop"; when the minimum lot does not fit, the robot does not enter.

More than half the trades closing at a loss is normal here: the profit comes from wins being twice the size of losses. It never trades against the reading. Calculations on past data are no guarantee they repeat; demo account first.

What does this panel do in the system's decisions?

The setup signals (Asia, New York · Setup page, Telegram, the MT5 robot's “Setup signals”) do not use this vote. They decide by their own tested rules: the daily and 4-hour trend scores (EMA50/200, EMA20 slope, RSI, MACD, swing structure), the session range, news windows and the range width.

Only the robot's “Reading” mode (it enters on the count of methods saying BUY or SELL), its “Day trader” mode (most methods must back the setup's side) and the Bot page's “Methods that must agree” filter use this panel. Otherwise it is a reference: the market seen from many angles.

BUY is a trade that profits if the price rises; SELL is a trade that profits if it falls. Gold can be traded either way.
One bar showing where the price opened and closed, and its high and low, over a set time (for example 15 minutes). Green rose, red fell.
How much time one candle covers: 15m, 1h, 4h, 1 day. Longer frames show the overall direction, shorter ones the entry.
The price's overall direction. Higher highs and higher lows make an uptrend; lower highs and lower lows a downtrend.
The trading hours of the world's main financial centres. Gold usually moves most in the London and New York hours. The site shows every time in your chosen time zone.
The gap between the buy and the sell price. A hidden cost paid on every trade; it widens around news.
Trade size. In gold 1 lot = 100 ounces, so a $1 move in gold is $100 on 1 lot and $1 on 0.01 lot. If you are new, start with the smallest lot.
The price that limits a loss: when it is reached the trade closes on its own. Setting one on every trade is how you know your risk.
The price where profit is taken: when it is reached the trade closes in profit.
The amount risked on one trade: the distance from entry to the stop. +2R is a profit twice the risk, −1R a full loss at the stop. A positive average R means the method made money over time.
The amount risked against the profit aimed for. 1 : 2 means risking $10 to make $20. Below 1, the win rate has to be high to come out ahead.
A practice account with no real money. Try the bot, the setups and your lot size here first, and move to a real account once you are used to them.
The broker's trading app (computer and phone). The site's bot runs inside MT5 and trades in your account.
Combines the trend on several timeframes into a score showing whether buyers or sellers have the upper hand. A lean, not a promise.
A line through the average price of the last 20, 50 or 200 candles, weighting recent prices more. Price above it usually means an uptrend, below it a downtrend.
Measures the speed of price moves from 0 to 100. Above 70 is read as overbought (risen too fast), below 30 as oversold.
Shows whether momentum is building or fading, from the gap between two EMAs.
Where the price sits within the range of the last few candles, from 0 to 100. Above 80 is near the top of the range, below 20 near the bottom.
Two bands set above and below an average by how much the price swings. Touching a band can mean the price has run far; narrow bands mean a quiet market.
A Japanese indicator that shows trend, support and resistance at once with a “cloud” and several lines. Price above the cloud leans up, below it leans down.
A channel drawn through the highest high and lowest low of the last few candles. A close outside it counts as a breakout.
Levels at 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and similar fractions of the last move. After a move, price often pulls back to one of them before carrying on.
Average True Range: how far one candle moves on average, in dollars. It shows how lively the market is; a stop sized by ATR fits both quiet and wild days.
Today's levels worked out from yesterday's high, low and close. R (resistance) is where a rise may stall, S (support) where a fall may stall, and the pivot sits between.
How fast and how strongly the price is moving one way. Fading momentum can be a sign the move is ending.
The price closing outside a range or level. A real breakout tends to carry on; a false one falls back into the range.
A way of reading where large players (banks, funds) place orders, using highs, lows and liquidity. A break in structure (MSS, BOS) hints that the direction may be changing.
Highs (BSL) and lows (SSL) where many traders' stops collect. A sweep is when the price briefly runs past such a level, takes those stops, and turns back.
A gap left inside three candles after a fast, strong move, where little traded. Price often comes back to fill it, so it is watched as an entry zone.
US jobs (NFP), inflation (CPI) and the Federal Reserve's rate decision (FOMC). When they come out, gold can move hard within minutes and spreads can widen.
Profit and loss: what the trades made or lost, added up.
The share of trades closed in profit. Not enough on its own: many small wins and a few big losses can still lose money. Read it with average R and profit factor.
Total profit divided by total loss. Above 1 is profitable: 1.5 means $1.50 made for every $1 lost. Below 1 is a loss.
The largest drop from a previous peak of the account. It shows how much was lost in the worst stretch, and whether you could sit through it.
How many days or trades a percentage is based on. A small count can be chance; under 30 the site shows no percentage.
